title: Of Friday's 547 paper trades, 422 were opened inside a 6-before, 3-after window around the jobs print. The agent that deployed the bots had no calendar. Should it get one, or should the human set the blackout?
author: QuanTradin
selftext:
Follow-up to yesterday's jobs-day post, because u/Patient_Ant_5409 said in the comments they use a 6 hour before, 3 hour after exclusion window around high-impact events. So I measured Friday against it.

Friday, 162k jobs against 55k expected. My 70 paper bots (19 of them actually traded) closed 547 trades for a loss of $1,820, paper money. 422 of those were opened between 2:30 am and 11:30 am ET, the window Patient\_Ant\_5409 described, and they account for $1,845 of the loss. The trades opened after 11:30 came out slightly ahead. 271 opened in the 9 o'clock hour alone, $1,712 of the loss.

The bots were deployed by an AI agent through our MCP server. It has 22 tools: build, backtest, deploy, read the desk, read the freeze. There is no calendar in there. The agent could not have known a report was due even if it had wanted to.

Two ways to fix it and I can't decide:

1. Give the agent a calendar tool and let it decide when to stand down.

2. Make the blackout a desk rule the human sets, which the agent can read but not lift, the same shape as the kill switch.

Which would you trust more, and what window would you set? Realised paper numbers, read off the desk this evening.

comments.author: Otherwise_Wave9374
comments.body: A calendar blackout is the right safeguard here, but I’d make it a policy engine instead of a hardcoded timer. Tie the agent’s order placement to event classes like jobs, CPI, FOMC, and earnings, then require an explicit override with a reason code when confidence is low. That gives you an audit trail and reduces silent failure when the agent is technically allowed to trade but shouldn’t. Agentix Labs would also benefit from logging the pre-trade context so you can separate strategy edge from schedule noise.
